Two-stage ROPE designs for single-arm non-inferiority and superiority trials

Riko Kelter
Institute of Medical Statistics and Computational Biology
Faculty of Medicine, University of Cologne
Cologne, Germany

28 October 2026

bfbin2arm-singlearm-twostage-rope-ni-superiority.rmd
library(bfbin2arm)

Overview

This vignette illustrates deterministic two-stage ROPE-based designs for single-arm phase II trials with binary endpoints. The functions design_singlearm_twostage_rope_ni() and design_singlearm_twostage_rope_sup() calibrate a design with one interim analysis and futility-only stopping.

The analysis prior is used to compute posterior ROPE probabilities, whereas the two design priors describe predictive scenarios under the null hypothesis H0H_0 and the desired hypothesis H1H_1. For a fixed clinical margin and set of evidence thresholds, the algorithm first determines the smallest feasible fixed-sample maximum size n*n^*. It then examines all allocations (n1,n2)(n_1,n_2) with n1+n2=n*n_1+n_2=n^* and selects the feasible allocation minimizing the expected sample size under the null design prior, EN0\mathrm{EN}_0.

At the interim analysis, continuation requires posterior support for the desired hypothesis to exceed 1−γ11-\gamma_1. Equivalently, the study stops for futility when posterior support for the null hypothesis is at least γ1\gamma_1.

Superiority example: HER2-positive gastric cancer

We first consider a superiority design motivated by a later-line HER2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal-junction cancer setting. Let the historical objective-response benchmark be p0=0.30p_0=0.30. A response-rate improvement of at least ten percentage points is considered clinically meaningful, giving the superiority boundary

p>p0+δsup=0.30+0.10=0.40. p > p_0 + \delta_{\mathrm{sup}} = 0.30 + 0.10 = 0.40.

The analysis prior is uniform. The null design prior is Beta(45,105)\mathrm{Beta}(45,105), centered at 0.30, representing non-superiority scenarios. The alternative design prior is Beta(44,36)\mathrm{Beta}(44,36), centered at 0.55, representing a clearly favorable superiority scenario. We use a final evidence threshold of 0.90 for superiority and for compelling evidence for non-superiority. At the interim, the trial stops for futility if posterior support for non-superiority is at least 0.80.

sup_2st <- design_singlearm_twostage_rope_sup(
  p0 = 0.30,
  delta = 0.10,
  analysis_prior = c(1, 1),
  design_prior_h0 = c(45, 105),
  design_prior_h1 = c(44, 36),
  gamma_1 = 0.80,
  gamma_eq = 0.90,
  gamma_diff = 0.90,
  alpha = 0.10,
  power = 0.80,
  pce = 0.60,
  alpha_freq = 0.10,
  power_freq = 0.80,
  p_t1e = 0.40,
  p_power = 0.55,
  nmax = 200,
  progress = FALSE
)

The summary function allows a convenient overview:

summary(sup_2st)

The selected design reports the maximum sample size n=n1+n2n=n_1+n_2, the continuation region at the interim analysis, predictive Bayesian power and type-I error, the probability of compelling evidence for non-superiority, and expected sample sizes under the two design priors.

The interim and final decision structures can be inspected graphically.

plot(sup_2st, type = "default")

Figure 1: Bayesian calibration of a single-arm two-stage ROPE-based clinical phase II trial with binary endpoints. The test used is a superiority test.

It is also possible to visualize and plot the interim and final continuation regions for the resulting design:

plot(sup_2st, type = "interim")
plot(sup_2st, type = "final")

Figure 2 and 3: Interim continuation and final decision regions for the single-arm two-stage ROPE superiority design.

This is helpful for monitoring a two-stage single-arm superiority trial: The first plot on the left shows that between 33 and 99 responses, out of 2020, the trial is continued (also compare the upper right panel in Fig. 1). The right plot shows that for the final n=68n=68 patients, superiority is declared when at least 3333 responses are observed.

Non-inferiority example: chemotherapy de-escalation

We next consider a non-inferiority design motivated by chemotherapy de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer. Let the historical pathological-complete-response benchmark be p0=0.50p_0=0.50. A loss of up to 15 percentage points is considered clinically acceptable in exchange for reduced chemotherapy exposure, giving the non-inferiority boundary

p≥p0−δNI=0.50−0.15=0.35. p \ge p_0-\delta_{\mathrm{NI}}=0.50-0.15=0.35.

We use a uniform analysis prior. The null design prior is Beta(20,60)\mathrm{Beta}(20,60), centered at 0.25, and represents clinically relevant inferiority. The alternative design prior is Beta(20,20)\mathrm{Beta}(20,20), centered at 0.50, and represents a plausible non-inferior efficacy scenario. We use γeq=0.925\gamma_{\mathrm{eq}}=0.925 to declare non-inferiority, γdiff=0.90\gamma_{\mathrm{diff}}=0.90 for compelling evidence of inferiority, and γ1=0.80\gamma_1=0.80 for interim futility.

ni_2st <- design_singlearm_twostage_rope_ni(
  p0 = 0.50,
  delta = 0.15,
  analysis_prior = c(1, 1),
  design_prior_h0 = c(20, 60),
  design_prior_h1 = c(20, 20),
  gamma_1 = 0.80,
  gamma_eq = 0.925,
  gamma_diff = 0.90,
  alpha = 0.10,
  power = 0.80,
  pce = 0.60,
  alpha_freq = 0.10,
  power_freq = 0.80,
  p_t1e = 0.35,
  p_power = 0.50,
  nmax = 200,
  progress = FALSE
)

We summarize the design:

Here, interim continuation requires

Pr⁡(p≥0.35∣Y1)>1−γ1=0.20. \Pr(p\ge 0.35\mid Y_1)>1-\gamma_1=0.20.

Equivalently, the trial stops early for futility if posterior support for clinically relevant inferiority, p<0.35p<0.35, is at least 0.80. At the final analysis, non-inferiority is declared when posterior support for p≥0.35p\ge0.35 is at least 0.925.

plot(ni_2st, type = "default")

Figure 1: Bayesian calibration of a single-arm two-stage ROPE-based clinical phase II trial with binary endpoints. The test used is a non-inferiority test. 

plot(ni_2st, type = "interim")
plot(ni_2st, type = "final")

Figure 2 and 3: Interim continuation and final decision regions for the single-arm two-stage ROPE non-inferiority design.

For this non-inferiority design, the trial continues after stage 1 when the observed number of responses belongs to C1={8,...,19}C_1 = \{8,...,19\}. The maximum sample size is n=90n=90, with n1=27n_1=27 patients enrolled before the interim analysis and n2=63n_2=63 additional patients enrolled after continuation.

Interpreting expected sample size

For both examples, the maximum sample size is n=n1+n2n=n_1+n_2, whereas the expected sample size under design-prior scenario j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\} is

ENj=n1+n2Prπj(d)(Y1∈C1). \mathrm{EN}_j=n_1+n_2\Pr_{\pi_j^{(d)}}(Y_1\in C_1).

The probability of stopping early for futility under each design scenario can be recovered from the expected sample size:

early_stop_prob <- function(design_object) {
  d <- design_object$design

  c(
    H0 = 1 - (d$EN0 - d$n1) / d$n2,
    H1 = 1 - (d$EN1 - d$n1) / d$n2
  )
}

rbind(
  superiority = early_stop_prob(sup_2st),
  noninferiority = early_stop_prob(ni_2st)
)
#>                       H0         H1
#> superiority    0.4246448 0.01291896
#> noninferiority 0.6317839 0.03448873

A large early-stop probability under H0H_0, together with a much smaller probability under H1H_1, is the intended operating profile of a futility-only two-stage design: the design conserves patients when the desired clinical claim is unlikely while preserving adequate predictive power when the desired hypothesis is plausible.

The generic function is also available when a programmatic workflow benefits from setting the decision direction explicitly:

design_singlearm_twostage_rope(
  p0 = 0.30,
  delta = 0.10,
  analysis_prior = c(1, 1),
  design_prior_h0 = c(45, 105),
  design_prior_h1 = c(44, 36),
  direction = "superiority"
)

Summary

This vignette illustrated simulation-free two-stage ROPE-based designs for single-arm phase II trials with binary endpoints in superiority and non-inferiority settings. Both examples use a single interim analysis with futility-only stopping and posterior ROPE probabilities as the evidence measure.

For the superiority illustration, the design evaluates whether the response probability exceeds the clinically meaningful boundary

p0+δsup=0.40. p_0+\delta_{\mathrm{sup}}=0.40.

The trial stops early for futility when posterior support for non-superiority is at least γ1=0.80\gamma_1=0.80, continues otherwise, and declares superiority at the final analysis when

Pr⁡(p>0.40∣Y)≥0.90. \Pr(p>0.40\mid Y)\ge0.90.

For the non-inferiority illustration, the design evaluates whether the response probability remains above

p0−δNI=0.35. p_0-\delta_{\mathrm{NI}}=0.35.

The trial stops early when posterior support for clinically relevant inferiority is at least γ1=0.80\gamma_1=0.80, and declares non-inferiority at the final analysis when

Pr⁡(p≥0.35∣Y)≥0.925. \Pr(p\ge0.35\mid Y)\ge0.925.

In both settings, the calibration algorithm first finds the smallest fixed-sample maximum size n⋆n^\star satisfying the selected operating characteristic constraints. It then evaluates every allocation (n1,n2)(n_1,n_2) satisfying

n1+n2=n⋆, n_1+n_2=n^\star,

and selects the feasible design with the smallest expected sample size under the null design prior, EN0\mathrm{EN}_0. The resulting design is therefore optimal conditional on the minimal feasible maximal sample size n⋆n^\star.

The main quantities to inspect after calibration are:

  • design$n1, design$n2, and design$n: the interim, second-stage, and maximum sample sizes.
  • design$type1_2st: predictive Bayesian type-I error under the null design prior.
  • design$power_2st: predictive Bayesian power under the alternative design prior.
  • design$pce_2st: probability of compelling evidence for the null hypothesis, including eligible interim and final evidence paths.
  • design$EN0 and design$EN1: expected sample sizes under the null and alternative design priors.
  • continuation_region: stage-1 response counts for which the trial continues to stage 2.
  • candidates: all feasible two-stage allocations considered for the fixed maximum sample size.

The generic function design_singlearm_twostage_rope() supports the same workflow through its direction argument. The convenience wrappers design_singlearm_twostage_rope_ni() and design_singlearm_twostage_rope_sup() provide direction-specific interfaces for non-inferiority and superiority designs, respectively.
